text: A small-time brewer is bludgeoned to death beside a quiet river, and nobody saw it happen. Detective Oh takes the case, and Lee Doo-yong gives him a hundred and fifty-eight minutes to work in, long enough that the film stops behaving like a procedural and turns into a winter journey, out through South Jeolla Province and back to Seoul, with the case reaching back into the war. The murder is small. The pursuit is not. What the running time buys is the sensation of a man walking through cold country putting questions to people who would rather he stopped, and the slow suspicion that the answer was fixed long before Yang died. It sits on the KOFA hundred as a case study in how much weight a detective story can take before it changes species.

Everything in this 1925 melodrama runs on money that belongs to somebody else. A young woman marries the disinherited son of a British aristocrat, and Frank Borzage builds ninety-six silent minutes on the plainest arithmetic the form owns: her position in the world depends entirely on men who keep failing at it, and the child is the one thing not yet taken out of her hands. The reversals are not really the point. What holds the picture is the way Borzage watches her absorb them, a small hardening, a trust extended to strangers because there is no alternative to trusting somebody. The class machinery is exact, too: an aristocratic family can decide it wants a grandson and simply begin taking steps, while her reply has to be improvised out of very little. The National Film Registry keeps it.

In 1992 men who had spent thirty years in South Korean prisons moved into Kim Dong-won's town, and he started filming them. He kept at it for twelve years, and that span is the substance of the picture. Not an interview but a long acquaintance: prisoners sent south as spies during the war become the old men he passes on the street, and their wish to go north stops sounding like a position and starts sounding like an elderly man's travel plan. A hundred and forty-nine minutes collects the ordinary hours a shorter film would cut, and it collects Kim's own difficulty as well, since he is host, neighbour and recorder at once and the camera does not pretend otherwise. Sundance gave it an award for freedom of expression; the film's own tone is quieter than that suggests, closer to visiting than to arguing.

A bass player waits for the City of New York to put him out of his loft, and his five-year-old daughter waits with him. Thomas Reichman filmed the wait in 1968: fifty-eight minutes in a room being emptied, with Charlie Mingus talking, playing, and dealing with the practical business of a man about to lose his address. There is music in it, and it is not a concert film. Eviction is a paperwork event, and the film's force comes from letting it stay one while the person it is happening to is a composer at full pressure, saying whatever occurs to him in front of a camera he seems to trust. The child in the room adjusts the register of everything said there. The National Film Registry keeps it, and the whole thing is over inside an hour.

The rule, as the film states it, was plain: at seventy a parent was carried up the mountain and left there. Kim Ki-young sets his 1963 film in the old kingdom of Goryeo, which lets him handle the practice as a working system rather than a horror, with sons who have already done it, sons whose turn is coming, and an economy in which one fewer mouth is a calculation somebody has made. Then a nobleman declines. Everything the picture has to say is in what that refusal costs him among neighbours who did not refuse, and in the fact that his mother can count as well as he can. A hundred and ten minutes, and the pressure never arrives from a villain; it comes from an agreement everyone keeps and nobody wants to be next under. It sits on KOFA's hundred Korean films.

Ten minutes of Charleston, South Carolina, in 1928: an orphanage band of Black children and teenagers, brass and drums, playing straight at a newsreel camera. Nobody made this to be a film. It was an item for the Fox Movietone reels, which is exactly why it repays sitting with, since the players are not acting, the framing has no ambitions, and what comes through is a group of young musicians who plainly know their business and know they are being recorded. There is no story here and no time for one. What survives is the playing, the faces, and the fact that somebody pointed a camera at this band on this day rather than at something more official. The National Film Registry took it in, which is an odd fate for a newsreel item and the correct one.

Twenty minutes, a poem, and a film cut to keep pace with it. Luis Valdez took a text about Chicano life in the United States and let the words do the structural work, so that images arrive as a response to lines rather than as scenes in a story. The result is closer to recitation than to explanation. Made in 1969, it shows little interest in introducing Chicano culture to strangers; it addresses people who already carry the history, and it moves at the tempo of a voice rather than of an argument. Twenty minutes also means it could travel: a reel, a projector, a room, an audience that does not have to be seated for two hours. The Academy Film Archive preserved it in 2017, which is how work made outside an industry stays available to be looked at rather than described.

A unit of marines wins its battle and then learns that the line has moved without them. What Lee Man-hee builds on that in 1963 is not a story of advance but of position: no contact with their own side, the Chinese army between them and it, and a hundred and ten minutes for men who have already spent their luck once. The interest sits with the group rather than the enemy. A war picture made in the country that fought the war, this close to it, tends to know unglamorous things, such as how fast an armed unit turns into a household, who talks too much, what gets said when there is no prospect of relief. KOFA's hundred Korean films keeps it, and the reason is visible in the premise alone: a few men, a landscape, and a situation nobody can walk out of.

Spring meltwater, and a river packed bank to bank with logs that have to be kept moving. Alfred Ames filmed the long drive in 1930: half an hour of hand-cut trees, horses hauling sleds over snow, and men standing on floating timber with a pole, working a current that will break a leg the moment they misjudge it. Nothing is arranged and there is nobody to root for. The film is an account of a sequence of jobs in the order they occur, from stump to mill to the boards and laths that come out the far end, and its value lies in its timing, since the methods it records had held for a century and a half and were on their way out. Nobody in the frame is performing for posterity. They are getting logs downstream before the water drops. Thirty minutes, on the National Film Registry.

A sleeping man is poor material for animation, so the interesting work happens before the nap. Will Vinton's Rip Van Winkle spends its energy on the walk: a lazy householder drifting away from his own door with a dog named Wolf, up into the Kaatskill mountains, into the company of strangers drinking and playing at bowls where nobody should be doing either. Animation earns its keep there. Figures who behave like men without quite being men, a brew handed over with no account of what it is, all of it presented rather than argued for. Twenty-seven minutes is long for a short, and the length goes into atmosphere instead of incident, which suits a story whose whole engine is a change nobody in it witnessed. The Academy Film Archive preserved it in 2013.

Two women, a century apart, both Black and both deaf; the film sets their lives beside each other and lets the rhyme carry the argument. Zeinabu irene Davis works from a structure rather than a plot, one strand in the early 1900s and one in the 1990s, ninety-three minutes divided between them, and what the pairing exposes is the point. Courtship turns out to be good historical evidence. How a woman is addressed, what work is open to her, who decides where she lives, whether the language she uses counts as a language: these shift unevenly between the two eras, and the film is careful about the unevenness rather than triumphant about it. The later half is not simply the corrected version of the earlier one, which is the harder thing to dramatize. It is on the National Film Registry.

A hundred minutes of two men in a ring, filmed in 1910 because a great many people expected the result to settle something outside it. The first Black heavyweight champion of the world, against a white former champion brought out of retirement: the fight was a proposition before it was a contest, and controversy attached to it immediately. What the footage offers is duration. Round after round shot at the pace of the event rather than shaped into a story, so that it has to be watched roughly the way the crowd watched it, over a long stretch, with the outcome still open. That is also what makes it a document. A staged fight can be reshot; this could not. The National Film Registry holds it, less for the boxing than for what a hundred minutes of it in 1910 was understood to mean.

The title puts the midwife first: these are her babies, and the account is hers. George C. Stoney filmed it in 1953 in the rural, segregated South, fifty-five minutes in households where a birth is attended by a woman who arrives with what she can carry. His interest is practical and unembarrassed about being practical, in what a room allows, what a family has, what can be done well anyway, and that practicality keeps the film from becoming a survey of poverty conducted from a comfortable distance. Conditions, good and bad, are the stated subject. The organizing presence, though, is a professional at work, and the film's regard for her competence does more argumentative work in 1953 than commentary could. It is on the National Film Registry.

Half of this is re-enactment and half is a man doing his rounds. Jerome Hill's 1957 film breaks at Schweitzer's thirtieth year: before it, Alsace, a childhood, a decision being reached, all staged for the camera; after it, the hospital-village in French Equatorial Africa, filmed across a single day, with a man in his eighties walking from building to building. The seam is the interesting part, because the two halves make different promises. One arranges a life into a choice. The other shows what the choice looks like fifty years on, at the speed of an ordinary working day. It won the Academy Award for documentary feature, and it also preserves the terms of its moment: the hospital arrives as the achievement of the man who built it, and the people around him are largely the setting for his day.
